From April through mid-June, maximum daily cooling energy increased to approximately 16–17 MWh, and during the summer, maximum daily cooling energy slightly decreased to around 15 MWh. The maximum daily cooling energy rose again to 16–17 MWh during the fall semester from September through mid- December. These patterns align with occupancy schedules developed by Bae et al. (2022), based on actual class reservation data collected from multiple U.S. universities, representing typical academic-year operations with reduced activity during weekends and summer months. To align the simulated cooling load profile with actual campus infrastructure, the Facundo Bueso building was selected as a representative case study. Functionally similar to the prototype model (e.g., classroom, laboratory, and administrative spaces), the modeled load profile provides a reasonable basis for scaling. In addition to the functional similarity, the prototype building’s maximum instantaneous cooling load was approximately 341.3 tons (1,200 kW), closely matching the Facundo Bueso building’s design maximum capacity of 350 tons and average operational load of 223.8 tons, obtained from the site visit. Using a scaling factor of 1.03, the prototype load profile was adjusted to reflect Facundo Bueso’s load magnitude. To evaluate system performance and cost-effectiveness at a district scale, the adjusted profile was further multiplied by four, representing a cluster of similar buildings (Figure 14c). This approach offers a practical and scalable method for comparing the existing chilled water plant with the proposed GeoSWAC concept under realistic, aggregated demand conditions. 23 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. The analysis boundary encompassed chiller units, cooling towers, circulating pumps, and connecting piping between chiller units and cooling towers, as well as between chillers and the campus loop. Capital and operational costs associated with the broader distribution network and in-building systems (e.g., air-handling units) were excluded to reduce uncertainty and maintain focus on core system components.
